lines.trans: Good evening, friends, and welcome back to Friday tea in Room Nine.
Thirty years ago in May, my aunt started a little waltz right at this piano.
Rain interrupted page two—until {F1} and {M1} opened these shutters again.
And tonight, our neighbour from number ten joins {F3} on the violin!
Ready on three, my friend? One, two, three...
Listen to the violin soar when the piano reaches middle D, {M2}!
Even my glasses are misty—and for once I know right where they are!
Look outside: people walking down {STREET} have stopped by the gate to listen!
And there is our gentle final chord, one octave high—home again.
Bravo! Bravo, {F3}! Hear the whole courtyard clapping!
Take a bow yourself, {M2}—your aunt's Friday room is alive again.
And nobody wants to go home yet—time for the cinnamon rolls!

meanings.note: Standard Arabic noun for 'evening', starting the universal greeting مساء الخير.

examples.trans: We used the word مساء.
This is another مساء.

meanings.note: Core word in صباح الخير ('good morning'), مساء الخير ('good evening'), تصبح على خير ('good night'), and rising-tone خير؟ ('is everything okay?').

examples.trans: Good morning, neighbours!

examples.text: خير إن شاء الله، شو صار؟
examples.trans: Hopefully all is well, what happened?

meanings.note: Placed directly before a name or title when addressing someone in Arabic (يا نور 'Nour!', يا أستاذ 'sir!') and in exclamations (يا سلام! 'wonderful!').

examples.trans: Good morning, Tariq!
Oh, how lovely the sun is after the rain!

meanings.note: Plural of صديق ('friend').

examples.trans: We used the word صديق.
This is another صديق.

meanings.note: Warm greeting used alone (أهلا!), with فيك/فيكي ('welcome to you!'), or paired as أهلا وسهلا! ('you are most welcome!').

examples.trans: Hello, I am Tariq!
Welcome to Jasmine House!

في.gloss: there is; there are; is there?

meanings.en: there is; there are; is there?
meanings.note: Spoken Levantine existential word ('there is / there are'); negated as ما في ('there is no / there are no').

examples.trans: There is a small paper tag on the handle.
There is nobody standing in the courtyard.

meanings.note: Everyday preposition meaning 'from', 'of', or 'than' after comparatives.

examples.trans: I am Salma from the kitchen.
Breakfast is from seven-thirty to ten.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: جديدة, plural: جداد).

examples.trans: I am Nour, the new receptionist.
I installed a new lightbulb last week.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun.

examples.trans: Please have a glass of hot mint tea.
There is black tea and coffee at breakfast.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: جمع.

examples.trans: The family gathers every Friday at noon.
On Friday the street is quiet.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: غرف.

examples.trans: We have eight comfortable rooms at the guesthouse.
Room four is ready and clean.

meanings.note: Numeral 'nine'; short form تسع (tisa') before a plural noun (تسع دقايق 'nine minutes').

examples.trans: The quietness in the courtyard is nine out of ten!
She came back in just nine minutes!

meanings.note: Means 'before' (قبل الفطور) and with a time span 'ago' (قبل ساعة 'an hour ago', قبل شوي 'just now').

examples.text: علمت بيانو هون قبل خمسة وعشرين سنة.
examples.trans: I taught piano here twenty-five years ago.
Drink your coffee before the rush.

meanings.note: Spoken Jordanian numeral 'thirty'.

examples.trans: They have given us thirty days in the letter.
The bill is thirty-eight dinars.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: سنين.

examples.trans: The building is eighty years old.
I have not seen him for three years.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: شهور.

examples.trans: That was the best sleep in a month!
The contract renews at the start of next month.

meanings.note: Jordan, Syria, Lebanon and Palestine use the old Syriac-derived month names: كانون التاني January ... أيار May ... أيلول September.

examples.trans: My birthday is in May.
In May the weather gets nice in Amman.

meanings.note: Arabic distinguishes father's sister (عمة, feminine of عمّ) from mother's sister (خالة).

examples.text: عمتي كانت تعزف عالبيانو كل يوم جمعة.
examples.trans: My paternal aunt used to play the piano every Friday.

examples.text: هاد الدفتر الأخضر هدية من عمتي.
examples.trans: This green notebook is a gift from my aunt.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (ببلش, بيبلش).

examples.trans: The brass pipe started heating up right away!
The clock tower started chiming twelve.

meanings.note: Musical loanword (from French valse) for a triple-time piano or orchestral waltz.

examples.text: عزفت سعاد فالس هادي بغرفة القزاز.
examples.trans: Suad played a gentle waltz in the sunroom.

examples.text: عنوان الورقة القديمة هو فالس الساحة.
examples.trans: The title on the old sheet is Courtyard Waltz.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: صغيرة, plural: صغار).

examples.trans: We found a little wooden train in the bag.
There are two small streets on the left.

meanings.note: Everyday preposition 'on, at, to'; before ال- it regularly contracts to عال- ('al- / 'a-).

examples.trans: Your glasses are on your forehead!
Say hello to Salma for me!

meanings.note: Spoken Jordanian demonstrative ('this / that'); feminine هادي (haadi), plural هدول (hadool). Before ال- it also contracts to هال-.

examples.trans: Here we use this big ledger.
This suitcase is very heavy today.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: بيانوهات.

examples.trans: The sound of the piano is warm and calm.
I learned piano when I was young.

meanings.note: Signature Jordanian/Palestinian pronunciation (with z) of بالضبط ('exactly!').

examples.trans: Exactly! You have become one of us.
Tell me exactly what to buy.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: أمطار.

examples.trans: Please come inside out of the cold rain.
The trees are green and lovely after the rain.

meanings.note: Past tense Arabic verb meaning 'to cut' or 'interrupt'.

examples.trans: We used the word قطع.
This is another قطع.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: صفحات.

examples.trans: Read the second page of the letter.
The notebook fell open to the middle page.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: تانية, plural: تانيين).

examples.trans: Room four is on the second floor.
There is a second sheet behind the letter.

meanings.note: Combines with ما before a verb to mean 'until' (لحد ما اتصلت 'until you called').

examples.trans: We waited until you called us.
I stayed up until midnight.

meanings.note: Negates verbs and في (ما بعرف 'I don't know', ما في 'there isn't'), and links conjunctions like قبل ما ('before') and بعد ما ('after').

examples.trans: Paper does not lose room names.
Have tea before you head out.

meanings.note: Appears in صباح النور ('morning of light', the standard reply to صباح الخير) and نور الشمس ('sunlight').

examples.trans: Good morning and welcome!
We read the card in the sunlight.

meanings.note: Male given name of the veteran handyman.

examples.trans: We used the word طارق.
This is another طارق.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بفتح, بيفتح).

examples.trans: The corner shop opens at seven.
Oh, the door finally opened!

meanings.note: Levantine word for slatted window shutters, used as a collective: الشيش مسكر 'the shutters are closed'.

examples.trans: Close the shutters, the sun is strong.
Green shutters suit the house.

meanings.note: Spoken Jordanian plural demonstrative ('these / those') for people or things.

examples.trans: Whose are these brass keys?
I have grown fond of those two rings!

meanings.note: Definite الليلة means 'tonight', while indefinite ليلة means 'one night / night of'.

examples.trans: I am going to sleep well tonight.
We booked the room for three nights.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: جيران.

examples.trans: All the neighbours on the street are kind.
Good morning, dear neighbour.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: أرقام.

examples.trans: Here is your key, room number four.
Is there a phone number written on the paper?

meanings.note: Numeral 'ten'; short form عشر ('ashar) before a plural noun (عشر دقايق 'ten minutes').

examples.trans: You arrived ten minutes early.
Breakfast is from seven-thirty to ten.

meanings.en: to take part; participate; share something with
meanings.note: Form III verb (بشارك / شارك). Often followed by بـ ('participate in') or مع ('share with').

examples.trans: All the neighbours took part in hanging the lanterns.
Share your new idea for the project with us.

meanings.note: Female given name of the retired piano teacher.

examples.trans: We used the word سعاد.
This is another سعاد.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun.

examples.trans: Piano playing calms the nerves.
Whenever she finishes playing, she smiles.

meanings.note: In Levantine Arabic, a noun for the violin (also pronounced كمنجة).

examples.trans: We used the word كمنجة.
This is another كمنجة.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: جاهزة, plural: جاهزين).

examples.trans: The desk is clean and the keys are ready.
Breakfast is ready in the courtyard.

meanings.note: Spoken Jordanian numeral 'three'; short form تلات (talaat) directly before a plural noun (تلات سنين 'three years').

examples.trans: Three years was a long time.
One, two, three!

meanings.note: Used both as the numeral 'one' and after a noun for emphasis ('a single, one and the same').

examples.trans: Not a single scratch on the cup!
The gate rang with one strong ring.

meanings.note: Spoken Jordanian numeral 'two' (إنتو التنين 'the two of you'); note homograph التنين ('Monday').

examples.trans: He has two left on the shelf.
Hold the torch, the two of you!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بسمع, بيسمع).

examples.trans: Did you hear the gate bell downstairs?
Inside the courtyard we hear the tree leaves.

meanings.note: Question word 'how?'.

examples.trans: How was the bus ride?
Tell me how to find the shop.

meanings.note: Intransitive verb ('ili / byi'la) describing a melody, voice, or price rising.

examples.text: بنص الأغنية، اللحن بيعلى شوي شوي.
examples.trans: In the middle of the song, the melody climbs bit by bit.
The sound of rain on the window grew louder at night.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian conjunction 'when' (in statements, not questions).

examples.trans: Smile when the bell rings!
When I get nervous, my sentences turn long.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بوصل, بيوصل).

examples.trans: Our guest arrived right on the second!
An official letter arrived at noon.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: نغمات.

examples.text: سمع كل نغمة من البيانو بهدوء.
examples.trans: He listened quietly to every note of the piano.
The chime of the bell is gentle, not harsh.

meanings.note: Solfege name standard in Arabic music education for the note D (ري الوسطى 'middle D').

examples.text: نغمة ري الوسطى هي المفتاح اللي كان ساكت.
examples.trans: Middle D is the exact key that was silent.

examples.text: الأغنية بتنزل بهدوء على نغمة ري بالأخير.
examples.trans: The song settles gently onto D near the end.

meanings.note: Feminine elative of وسط (middle), agreeing with نغمة for 'middle D'.

examples.trans: We used the word أوسط.
This is another أوسط.

meanings.note: Male given name of the guesthouse owner.

examples.trans: We used the word مازن.
This is another مازن.

meanings.note: Before a noun or clause حتى means 'even' (حتى والغرفة فاضية 'even when the room is empty').

examples.text: حتى والغرفة فاضية، السلك بيرن مرتين.
examples.trans: Even when the room is empty, the wire rings twice.
Even room four's bell went quiet!

meanings.note: In Levantine Arabic, a noun for eyeglasses (usually plural in Arabic), with 'my'.

examples.trans: We used the word نضارة.
This is another نضارة.

meanings.note: Feminine Levantine Arabic word meaning 'misty', 'foggy', or 'blurry'.

examples.trans: We used the word مغبّش.
This is another مغبّش.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: مرات.

examples.trans: The doorbell rang twice.
I read the letter three times.

meanings.note: Arabic very often uses the active participle عارف ('knowing') for the present 'I know'.

examples.trans: We used the word عارف.
This is another عارف.

meanings.note: Spoken Jordanian question word for 'where?'.

examples.trans: Where is the computer, Tariq?
Where should I put the small spoons?

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: أماكن.

examples.trans: This place is very quiet and comfortable.
Everything is tidy in its proper place.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb for 'to see, look, check' (بشوف / شاف).

examples.trans: Look inside the suitcase, Nour!
I will see you tomorrow at breakfast.

meanings.note: Used both before a noun ('outside the gate') and standalone ('outside').

examples.trans: It is raining outside.
A yellow taxi stopped outside the gate.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: ناس.

examples.trans: You are kind, generous people.
Morning coffee brings people together in the courtyard.

meanings.note: Invariant spoken Jordanian relative pronoun ('who, which, that') for any gender or number.

examples.trans: That is what I want.
The inn that keeps a stranger's bag safe.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: ماشية, plural: ماشيين).

examples.trans: I saw my brother walking down this street.
Everything is going smoothly.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: شوارع.

examples.trans: Our guesthouse is on a quiet street in central Amman.
There are old stone streets in the quarter.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: ياسمين.

examples.trans: The jasmine vine climbs above the door.
The evening scent of jasmine lifts the spirit.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بوقف, بيوقف).

examples.trans: A yellow taxi stopped outside the gate!
My heart stopped at page one!

meanings.note: Marks location ('at, by') and with pronoun suffixes expresses possession: عندي ('I have'), عندك ('you have'), عندنا ('we have').

examples.trans: A taxi just stopped at the door.
I have a reservation under the name Suad.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: بوابات.

examples.trans: The courtyard gate is open for guests.
The taxi stopped outside the gate.

عشان.gloss: for; because of; in order to

meanings.en: for; because of; in order to
meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian word for 'for / because of' (عشان هيك 'that is why') and 'so that'.

examples.trans: That is why the suitcase was heavy!
Are you polishing the lanterns for noon?

meanings.note: Placed directly before an indefinite noun without ال- to mean 'the last' (آخر يوم 'the last day', آخر الساحة 'the far end of the courtyard').

examples.trans: The attic room is at the end of the floor.
Today is the last day of the week.

meanings.note: Masculine هادي ('quiet') is homographic with the feminine demonstrative هادي ('this'); context and agreement distinguish them cleanly.

examples.trans: The spot above the tree is very quiet.
We prepared the quiet attic room for you.

meanings.note: Musical interval of eight scale steps.

examples.text: مدام سعاد عزفت نفس اللحن أوكتاف أعلى.
examples.trans: Madam Suad played the same melody one octave higher.

examples.text: الأوكتاف الوسطاني بالبيانو بده دوزان بسيط.
examples.trans: The middle octave on the piano needs a light tuning.

meanings.note: Used both before a noun ('above, over') and standalone ('upstairs').

examples.trans: The window is above the old tree.
Let us go upstairs to see the room.

رجع.gloss: to return; come back; start again

meanings.en: to return; come back; start again
meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (برجع, بيرجع).

examples.trans: Can you run there and come back in ten minutes?
Did the pipe start dripping again?

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: بيوت.

examples.trans: The old house has a lovely courtyard.
The neighbourhood houses are built of stone.

meanings.note: Commonly heard in Amman to applaud music, baking, or a clever idea. Followed by عليك/عليكي for 'well done to you!'.

examples.trans: Bravo! The piano playing was wonderful!

examples.text: برافو عليكي يا نور، الخطة ممتازة.
examples.trans: Well done, Nour, the plan is excellent.

meanings.note: Before an indefinite singular noun كل means 'every' (كل يوم 'every day'); before a definite noun it means 'all / the whole' (كل الأسبوع 'all week').

examples.trans: Tell me everything I need to know.
Everyone is happy in the courtyard today.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: ساحات.

examples.trans: The courtyard has a big jasmine tree.
We sat drinking tea in the courtyard.

meanings.note: Levantine progressive marker placed before a present-tense verb to show action happening right now.

examples.trans: The water is flowing inside the pipe right now!

examples.text: كنت عم بدور على دفتري هلا.
examples.trans: I was just looking for my notebook.

meanings.note: Clap your hands, or clap for a performer at the end.

examples.trans: People clapped a lot after the song.
Clap twice and the lamp lights up.

meanings.note: Common Arabic verb meaning 'to bow down' or take a theatrical bow.

examples.trans: We used the word انحنى.
This is another انحنى.

meanings.note: Spoken Jordanian pronoun 'you' when addressing one man.

examples.trans: Did you plant these herbs yourself?
Did you plan this entire meeting?

كمان.gloss: also; too; again (كمان مرة once more)

meanings.en: also; too; again (كمان مرة once more)
meanings.note: Everyday Levantine word for 'also, too, more' (كمان مرة 'one more time / again').

examples.text: التفكير السريع أنقذ الفطور كمان مرة!
examples.trans: Quick thinking saved breakfast once again!
And I missed you too.

meanings.note: Spoken Jordanian possessive word ('belonging to'); agrees in gender: تبع (m.), تبعت (f.), تبعون (pl.).

examples.text: اليوم آخر يوم بأسبوع التجربة تبعك.
examples.trans: Today is the last day of your trial week.
My brother's piano teacher!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun.

examples.trans: Life is sweet with kind people.
Never in my life have I seen a prettier view.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian word for 'someone / anyone'; with ما في (ما في حدا) it means 'nobody'.

examples.trans: Someone rang the gate bell!
There is nobody standing in the courtyard.

meanings.note: Signature Levantine word for 'want / need', inflected with pronoun suffixes: بدي (I want), بدك (you want), بده (he/it wants), بدها (she/it wants), بدنا (we want), بدكم (you pl. want), بدهم (they want).

examples.trans: I want to read the booking ledger.
Jam bread needs unsalted butter.

meanings.note: Everyday Levantine Arabic Arabic verb روّح specifically meaning 'to go home'.

examples.trans: We used the word روّح.
This is another روّح.

meanings.note: Means 'still' in affirmative sentences (لسا سليم 'still intact') and 'not yet' alone or with negation (لسا؟ 'not yet?').

examples.trans: Is your cup still intact?
Nobody has written anything yet.

meanings.note: Core Jordanian everyday verb for 'to come' (إجا / بيجي).

examples.trans: You came ten minutes early.
I will come on Friday at noon.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: أوقات.

examples.trans: Old pipes take time to warm up.
You arrived right on time.

meanings.note: Plural of لفافة ('roll/scroll'), used in bakeries for cinnamon rolls.

examples.trans: We used the word لفافة.
This is another لفافة.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun.

examples.trans: The warm scent of cinnamon filled the kitchen.
We ate a cinnamon roll with tea.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: قريبة, plural: قراب).

examples.text: علمت بيانو ببيت قريب من هون.
examples.trans: I taught piano in a house near here.
We booked a table at a nearby restaurant.
